relations.reason: Topology/neighborhood and producer-resource-consumer handoff are distinct tasks over the same exchange semantics.
Graph explains selected paths; matrix survives dense global pairwise coverage.
Both answer workflow/ownership; BPMN should replace simple lanes only when events, gateways, exceptions, or choreography semantics earn the notation cost.
Sequence optimizes participant/message order while timeline optimizes duration, overlap, and clock time.
Bounded comprehension and large-scale lookup/progressive disclosure are different tasks.
Gantt/roadmap exposes duration and slippage while dependency graph exposes causal schedule structure.
Matrix is strongest for coverage/completeness; graph is strongest for selected impact neighborhoods.
Use the composite only when several complementary operations are first-class; otherwise a simpler collection plus inspector is cheaper.
Use Sankey/alluvial only when magnitude is semantically meaningful; otherwise ordinary topology should win.

Both show what moves between steps; use the port graph only when named, typed inputs and outputs per step matter (Zapier/n8n/Node-RED style), otherwise a producer-resource-consumer handoff is lighter.
A port graph is a node-link graph whose edges attach to named ports and carry a typed payload; plain topology wins when what passes along an edge does not matter.

Layers and C4 levels answer where a part sits; a component diagram answers what each part provides and requires through its interfaces. Generate both from one model rather than drawing either by hand.
Use a UML class diagram when operations, inheritance, or realized interfaces of code types matter; use the data-model diagram for persisted entities, attributes, and cardinality.
Both compare one quantity across categories; dot plots suit many categories or values far from zero, bars suit few categories with a meaningful zero.
The bar chart shows rank and size at a glance; the table carries exact values and the extra columns a reader looks up afterwards.
A line chart shows how a quantity changes over time; a timeline shows when discrete events happened. Pages about change often need both on one time axis.
Both show how two variables relate; a scatter plot keeps individual items, a heatmap bins them when there are too many points to read.
A dot plot compares one measure across categories; small multiples repeat that comparison for each group so the groups can be compared side by side.
Both walk one mechanism step by step; the staged machine lets the viewer step and probe, the clip plays by itself where nobody can click (a deck, an email, a feed).
Animation shows that something changed; side-by-side stills let a reader compare the states exactly (Robertson et al. 2008), so a clip about change pairs with small multiples for analysis.
Both are grids of pairwise links; the traceability matrix when rows and columns are different kinds (requirement x test), the adjacency matrix when they are the same kind.
The composite is a container of linked panes; the table is the pane for exact, sortable values.
The composite is a container of linked panes; the port graph is the pane that shows which interface connects to which.
The composite is a container of linked panes; the schema explorer is the pane for browsing entity types and their fields.
The composite is a container of linked panes; the state map is the pane that shows every state and transition.
The flow shows who hands what to whom; the table gives each handoff's exact attributes.

The matrix shows coverage gaps at a glance; the table gives each item's exact fields.
The schema explorer shows the structure (entity types, fields, links); the table shows the rows.

For an ordered first-match-wins rule chain, a decision table shows every rule's conditions side by side and its evaluation order as row order; a flowchart spreads the same rules across branches the reader must trace (issue #2, interview-kit c9641e9).
A process model of nested gateways and a decision table both encode the same rule chain; DMN separates them precisely so the decision logic is read as a table and the process only references it.
A data table lists records; a decision table lists rules whose order decides the outcome. A page can show the rules and the records they classified together.
A state machine shows which state follows which; a decision table shows the conditions that choose a transition or outcome.
A traceability matrix shows which requirement covers which item; a decision table shows which conditions produce which outcome. A rule set can be traced to the requirements that motivated each rule.

Both list items to pick from. When each item's only detail is a link elsewhere, master-detail's inspector pane has nothing to hold; a link directory makes every row the link (skill rating 2026-10-01). When items have fields to read on the page, master-detail is the fit.
A table earns its columns when readers sort or compare fields; a list of places to go has one field worth reading, so a grouped link list says the same with less.
A tree shows how the groups nest; a link directory lists each group's destinations. A large index can use the tree as its table of contents.

Both read top to bottom. A scroll-linked explainer walks one mechanism through its steps; an argument page makes a case, each section proving one claim. A page that persuades rather than teaches a mechanism is an argument page (skill rating 2026-09-25: graph and flow views ranked first for narrative portfolio pages).
A staged machine can be the evidence for one section of an argument page, the section that claims how something works.
A graph can back one section's claim about how parts connect; it does not carry the page's argument by itself.

Both put one dot per item on a shared scale. When each value is an estimate with a range, the interval plot draws the range and a reference line, so the reader sees which items are clearly different and which only look different (skill rating 2026-09-30).
A bar chart shows amounts from zero; error bars on top of bars invite reading the bar's length as certain. Estimates with uncertainty read better as a dot and an interval line.

Both colour a grid by value. A heatmap's one-hue scale suits amounts from zero up; values that go either way from zero need a diverging scale centred on grey at zero, or the sign is lost (skill rating 2026-09-30).
The matrix shows which cause moves which outcome and in which direction; the interval plot shows, for one row or column, how sure each effect is.

Both can show a run. A staged machine teaches how the system works step by step; an answer-receipt card shows what one run answered and the evidence and receipt behind it. A live-demo result panel is the card (skill rating 2026-09-29: the router returned a staged machine for it).
A portfolio page argues a claim; a run's answer-receipt card is checkable evidence for one of its sections.
Several runs' cards in one shared layout read as small multiples: the same slots in the same places, so differences between runs stand out.
